The power stack is moving out of the 
compute rack
Rapidly rising AI rack density is forcing a redesign of how power is 
delivered to the compute

NVIDIA rack power has increased from roughly 45kW for Hopper to 120-140kW for 
Blackwell, while our model reaches 225-275kW for Rubin class systems and future 
systems could move up to 500kW-1MW+. Higher power per accelerator, more 
accelerators per scale-up domain and increased networking are all contributing to this 
increase. 
The challenge is that today's racks typically distribute power internally at only 48-54V. As 
rack power rises, delivering the same watts at low voltage requires dramatically more 
current. That requires larger copper busbars and cables, higher resistive loses and heat, 
more difficult connectors and protection and more rack space devoted to power rather 
than compute. At several hundred kW per rack, continuing to scale the low-voltage 
architecture becomes increasingly uneconomic. 
We expect the power architecture to evolve through a 4-stage 
transition
With the rise in rack power, we see the bulky AC/DC conversion, energy storage, 
protection and system controls progressively moving  upstream into dedicated power 
shelves and power racks, allowing higher-voltage DC to travel deeper into the compute 
rack at much lower current.  Longer term, industry participants are driving toward native 
800V architectures carrying high voltage directly toward the compute node, with DC/DC 
conversion occurring close to the accelerator. 
We view the transition to 800V architectures enable higher rack densities and 
ultimately GW-scale AI clusters, while also shifting and adding value across the 
power supply chain. Content increases in high-voltage AC/DC rectification, battery 
and capacitor backup, AC and DC power distribution, controls and additional DC/DC 
conversion stages. Even in the native 800V architecture, higher-value opportunities 
remain in node-level conversion, protection and safety controls. 
A few factors driving the change: 
1. Low-voltage current becomes increasingly difficult to manage. Power 
equals voltage x current. A 250kW rack supplied at 50V requires roughly 5,000A; 
at 800V the same load only requires ~313A.  The high current requires much more 
copper, increases resistive losses and heats and makes the connectors, busbars and 
fault management harder. 
2. Power hardware competes with compute for valuable rack space.  Today's 
systems contain server PSUs or rack-level power shelves, busbars, capacitors and 
controllers that occupy space otherwise available for GPUs, CPUs, networking and 
cooling. Moving bulky power hardware upstream or into adjacent power racks 
frees valuable compute space and simplifies servicing. 
3. High voltage distribution is more efficient.  Resistive loss increases with the 
square of current. Reducing current lowers the copper requirements and 
distribution losses, while allowing more power to be delivered through the cables 
and connectors. 
4. Energy storage is becoming more tightly integrated into AI power 
architecture. Large synchronized training and inference workloads can create 
rapid changes and surges to demand. Centralizing batteries, capacitors and 
controls allow power to be buffered and managed across multiple compute racks 
rather than independently inside each rack.

The architecture is migrating through four overlapping 
stages
We expect AI power delivery to migrate through an evolutionary transition to a fully 
native 800VDC architecture between now and the end of the decade.  The infrastructure 
should upgrade as the hardware upgrades to higher power systems, safety standards 
mature and the industry develops reliable power delivery to meet each upgrade stage.  
We view a staged transition over time for the AC/DC conversion, energy storage and 
controls to navigate upstream while higher voltage DC is carried progressively deeper 
into the IT rack toward a high ratio DC/DC stage closer to the accelerator.  
We see the progression through the following stages: 
1. Distributed server PSUs: The first stage of AI hardware which persisted through 
NVIDIA's Ampere and Hopper generation and early ASIC accelerator racks from 
2021-2024, the 415/480VAC reached the IT rack through the busway. Once inside 
the server, it was converted with an AC-DC power supply unit (PSU) to 12V or 
48VDC before board-level point-of-load regulation by a DC-DC module. The 
server PSUs still carry on with general CPU servers using this architecture.
2. Centralized rack power shelf. In the 2nd stage which is now industry 
mainstream for the NVIDIA Blackwell generation and ASIC rack hardware from 
Google and Amazon, server-level AC/DC conversion consolidates into a rack-level 
power shelf feeding a 48/54VDC busbar. The downstream 48V-to-12V-to-core-
voltage conversion chain remains largely unchanged.
3. 400+/- and 800VDC power rack. In the upcoming stage that would see initial 
shipments from late 2026-27 alongside Rubin and upcoming ASIC racks from 
Google, Amazon, and Meta, we see adjacent power racks converting 
415/480VAC to 400+/-VDC or 800VDC. As an evolutionary step, these power 
racks could upgrade to larger row level power blocks (2.5MW) or facility level 
power centers (6.5MW) to deliver power to multiple IT racks. The power rack 
centralizes the DC link, ride-through or energy storage, protection and system 
controls. In the upcoming generation, transitional designs step the 800V power 
inside the rack to 48/54V inside the IT rack. Once it matures further, more native 
designs will carry 800V through a busbar deeper into the rack and perform high-
ratio conversion down to low voltage close to the compute node.   
4. Potential SST end-state: We see development underway to consolidate the 
medium voltage transformer and rectification later in the decade with a solid-state 
transformer (SST). The SST converts the medium-voltage AC directly to isolated 
800VDC for distribution across the data hall, replacing the conventional line-
frequency transformer and separate downstream rectification stages. Once inside 
the rack, an 800V busbar can span the system to deliver power to the server board 
for high ratio conversion to low voltage for use by the GPU. 
   We view the transition to high-voltage DC redistributing the power stack rather than 
eliminating it. The 800V power-rack phase may initially be additive to content per watt, 
as centralized rectification, storage, protection, controls and HVDC distribution are 
introduced while much of the existing low-voltage chain remains. Native 800V later 
removes the intermediate 48/54V layer, but raises the value and technical requirements 
of high-ratio node-level DC/DC conversion, high-voltage protection, connectors, 
busbars and telemetry. We therefore see a barbell of opportunity in larger centralized 
power systems upstream and higher-value conversion and protection close to the silicon 
downstream.

The following section breaks down which components are added, retained or removed 
at each transition, and the resulting implications for content per rack and content per 
watt.
800V offers power electronics content expansion 
The transition to higher-voltage DC alters both the placement of power hardware and 
the sources of value creation. In current architectures, a significant share of conversion, 
short-duration backup, and low-voltage distribution is housed within the IT rack. As rack 
density increases, the larger and less space-efficient elements of the power stack 
gradually shift upstream—initially to centralized rack power shelves, then to nearby 
800V power racks, and eventually to row- or facility-level conversion. Meanwhile, the 
final DC/DC conversion required by the accelerator moves in the opposite direction, 
increasingly closer to the silicon.
We view the 800V offering a step-up of power electronics on a per watt basis.  The 
transition offers new content in high voltage rectification, energy storage, DC 
distribution, protection and near-chip DC/DC conversion which more than offsets some 
mid-term elimination of low voltage AC-DC components. 
NVIDIA's published roadmap and its discussions at GTC (link) and OCP  Asia (link) show it 
actively driving its supply chain toward a phased transition to 800V DC.  It introduced 
MGX compatible 800VDC power rack to start initial production alongside Rubin and 
mid-term is developing with the power supply vendors row-level power centers using 
800VDC busways and longer-term facility scale DC power blocks that convert medium 
voltage power directly to 800VDC.

Major components of the AI power BOM
We summarize the power chain into five major content buckets:
1. AC-to-DC power conversion. Historically AC to DC conversion was handled by 
individual PSUs but is increasingly centralized within rack-level power shelves. 
With the move to 800V architecture, the PSUs would shift into a dedicated power 
rack and longer term into facility level conversion such as an SST. 
2. Energy storage and ride-through. Energy storage systems including battery 
back-up units (BBUs), capacitor back-up units (CBUs) or supercapacitor shelves 
provide continuity during short disturbances and buffer the rapid power changes 
generated by large synchronized AI workloads. The architectural change is 
increasingly toward pooling this capacity across multiple compute trays or racks 
rather than duplicating it inside each server. For 800V, centralized BESS (battery 
energy storage systems) could provide back-up power to the 800V busway to 
deliver to the IT racks. 
3. Distribution, protection and controls. The power distribution network includes 
busbars, cables, input and output PDUs, disconnects, fuses/contactors, pre-charge 
circuitry, isolation monitoring and power-management controllers. These 
components rise in importance at 800V because DC fault interruption, safe 
servicing and protection coordination become more demanding. 
4. Intermediate DC/DC conversion. The DC-DC conversion takes the distribution 
voltage down to a level that can be handled near the compute tray holding the 
accelerators. Today this often means converting 48/54V to ~12V. During the initial 
800V transition it can mean converting 800V to 48/54V followed by the existing 
48/54V-to-12V stage. In a more native architecture, the intermediate 48/54V layer 
can disappear and a high-ratio converter takes 800V directly toward ~12V near 
the compute node.
5. Point-of-load (POL) voltage regulator modules (VRMs) as the last 
conversion step. The POL VRMs take the intermediate voltage down to the very 
low core voltage power required by the GPU, CPU and memory. The value of 
conversion immediately adjacent to increasingly expensive processors becomes 
more critical. Vertical power delivery is starting to move the VRM from beside the 
accelerator to the backside of the PCB directly beneath it, sharply shortening the 
high current, low-voltage path. We see the transition first from ASICs from 
Amazon and Google and extending to NVIDIA from the Feynman generation. 

We discuss the architecture transition from current systems through the coming years 
moving toward facility level 800V power distribution. 
Stage 1: Distributed server power for smaller systems with 
tens of kW
Early AI GPU platforms including Ampere and Hopper and many first-generation ASIC 
systems use a distributed power architecture. Facility AC is delivered to the rack and split 
among individual server or compute-tray power supply units. Each PSU converts the AC 
input to a 12–50V intermediate bus, after which board-level DC/DC converters and 
point-of-load voltage regulator modules generate the low-voltage rails required by the 
processor, memory and other components.
This architecture is modular and straightforward to service, but repeats rectifiers, bulk 
capacitors, fans, controllers and input cabling across each server. That duplication is 
manageable when rack loads remain in the tens of kilowatts, with power continuity 
generally provided by upstream UPS and generator infrastructure rather than large 
amounts of dedicated rack-level storage. As rack power rises, however, a growing share 
of rack volume, airflow and copper is consumed by power hardware rather than 
compute. The opportunity in this stage is therefore dominated by conventional PSUs and 
board-level conversion: absolute content rises with server wattage, but there is relatively 
little architectural content expansion. 
In our current model, a Hopper-class rack contains roughly US$19k of rack-to-chip 
power-electronics content, including approximately US$13k of server PSU content. We 
use this as the baseline against which the larger power shelves, energy storage, 
protection and DC/DC content introduced in subsequent stages are measured.
Stage 2: Shift to centralized 48/54V power shelves for more 
free server space 
Blackwell and many current CSP ASIC architectures move AC/DC conversion out of 
individual compute trays and into shared rack-level power shelves. Modular PSUs 
operate in parallel and feed a common 48/54V busbar, while intermediate bus 
converters and VRMs remain within the compute trays and continue stepping voltage 
down toward the accelerator. This reduces duplicated conversion hardware, makes 
modules easier to service and frees more of the server chassis for compute.

provisioning margin. We therefore view Jalapeño’s higher PSU content as primarily a

Higher power-shelf complexity keep the PSUs from commoditizing
The move from a 5.5kW module to an 18.3kW module is more than an increase in 
component count. At this level, suppliers must combine three-phase power-factor 
correction, high-efficiency isolated conversion, greater heat-flux management, fast 
response to AI workload transients, active current sharing, hot-swap capability, 
redundancy, telemetry and coordinated protection within a tightly constrained rack 
form factor.
Infineon’s 18kW reference design illustrates the engineering required: it targets 97.5% 
peak efficiency, roughly 100W/in³ power density, 20ms of integrated hold-up and 
support for electrical design peak loads of up to 180%. It also uses SiC and GaN devices, 
advanced magnetics and real-time digital control. At 18.3kW, even a 0.5 percentage-
point efficiency difference equates to approximately 92W of additional heat per module, 
or more than 500W across six modules. Efficiency, transient performance and thermal 
reliability therefore have direct consequences for rack density and operating cost. 
Power shelves also need to operate as part of a larger system. The supplier must manage 
parallel operation, droop or active current sharing, N+1 redundancy, high-power-factor 
performance under dynamic GPU loads, shelf-level monitoring and communication with 
the BBU, PMM and rack controller. These requirements, combined with platform 
qualification and customer-specific validation, differentiate higher-power shelves from 
lower-value commodity power products. 

Despite these improvements, 48/54V distribution eventually reaches a physical limit. A 
200kW load at 50V requires roughly 4,000A, while a 1MW load would require 
approximately 20,000A. The resulting busbars, connectors and copper become too 
large, heavy and lossy, and the number of power shelves begins to consume a material 
share of the IT rack. In our current configuration, GB200/GB300 already requires 
multiple 33kW shelves; extending the same approach toward a megawatt would be 
impractical. 
Additional Rack Level Energy storage (BBUs/CBUs) is 
optional
The transition to rack-level shelves also creates a natural location for energy storage, but 
not every deployment requires the same solution. Solutions can span capacitors close to 
the rack for rapid support of GPU power swings to BESS near the utility connection for 
longer-duration load averaging and support during extended periods of power loss. 
 PSU-integrated capacitors: Capacitors integrated in the power shelf provide the 
fastest transient response and tens of milliseconds of hold-up.
 CBU / power-capacitance shelf. A CBU shelf can provide 0.1 seconds to several 
seconds of high-power workload smoothing.
 BBU (Battery Back-up Unit): Provides tens of seconds to several minutes of 
power-loss ride-through.  These are more efficient for longer events over the CBU. 
 UPS / BESS: Facility-level battery energy storage systems for resilience, generator 
transfer, load averaging and grid services.
We distinguish three implementations: batteries distributed within IT racks; BBUs 
consolidated into a dedicated power rack supporting one or more IT racks; and pooled 
batteries serving a row or facility through UPS or DC-storage infrastructure.  Delta’s 
demonstrated 660kW 800V power rack integrates 480kW of battery backup, while Lite-
On has also shown an 800V power rack with integrated BBU. 
These designs demonstrate that high-voltage distribution and power-rack batteries can 
coexist with the storage architecture flexible for data center operators. Some data 
centers will retain a centralized AC UPS and may need only the PSU’s embedded buffer 
or a CBU for workload smoothing. Other data center operators may remove part of the 
UPS layer and use rack- or row-level BBUs for backup-source transfer. Some 
configurations will use both CBU and BBU because they solve different time-duration 
problems. A newer PSU may also integrate sufficient energy buffering to eliminate a 
separate capacitor shelf for part of the workload envelope. Infineon, for example, says 
its integrated energy-buffer design can reduce required capacitor volume and avoid a 
separate capacitor bank in some implementations. 
Moving backup further upstream creates greater potential to reduce dedicated rack-
level battery capacity, while retaining local capacitors or other fast buffers. Feedback 
from our Samsung SDI analyst, Tim Bush, points to some data centers transitioning 
toward pooled prismatic lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries in UPS applications 
starting from Rubin/Rubin Ultra-era deployments. Customer qualification and the 
chosen facility power design will determine the adoption path whether pooling or 
staying near the rack. Our market feedback suggests hyperscalers more often rely on 
BBU to maintain better stability for their training and inference clusters alongside 
capacitor shelves for better smoothing of voltage while the broader enterprise and 
smaller operators have UPS and generators.  
The supply chain for a BBU includes the battery maker including Panasonic Energy, 
Samsung SDI and CATL and battery pack suppliers Dynapack, AES and STL before going 
to a system maker such as Delta or Lite-On for integration.  For battery chemistry, LFP is 
itself a lithium-ion chemistry with safety and cycle-life characteristics that can be 
attractive for frequently cycled, pooled storage, although lower energy density can 
require more space for the same runtime. High-output cylindrical cells remain relevant 
where compactness and power delivery are priorities. The choice therefore depends on 
discharge power, duration, cycling, footprint and safety requirements—not simply 
whether the system operates at 800V. 

Panasonic and Samsung SDI have different emphasis on pooled vs. rack level 
batteries
Panasonic has portrayed a positive outlook for its energy storage with portfolio leading 
on in-rack cylindrical batteries and targeting the growing BBU shelf opportunity in the 
power rack. Its disclosed roadmap includes higher-output BBUs, BBUs for power racks 
and CBUs, with HVDC-compatible BBUs and first-generation CBUs scheduled to begin 
mass production within the fiscal year ending March 2027. Panasonic also states that 
products included in its medium-term sales plan have secured customer awards, which it 
defines as agreements covering development initiatives and orders. This supports 
continued distributed-storage opportunities even as some backup shifts upstream. 
Samsung SDI has exposure to both distributed and centralized battery demand. Its 
current portfolio includes high-nickel cylindrical BBU cells and prismatic lithium-
manganese-oxide UPS batteries, while it is preparing prismatic LFP production for ESS 
and UPS applications. Its July results also outlined expansion of high-power cylindrical 
capacity for BBU demand into the US. We therefore see SDI as positioned to pursue a 
chemistry and location shift, rather than requiring conventional BBUs to disappear. 
Panasonic, meanwhile, sells modules and storage-system solutions as well as cells; its 
revenue opportunity should not be compared directly with cell-only BBU market 
estimates. 
Power supply vendors: Delta and Lite-On still have value in energy storage 
integration
Even where the underlying cells are purchased from a third party, the BBU is a qualified 
power-electronics and safety subsystem. The vendor integrates bidirectional charger, 
battery management, contactors, fuses, disconnect and fault isolation, thermal 
management, shelf controls, telemetry and rack level communications and mechanical 
integration, serviceability and lifetime assurance. 
The value added by Delta or Lite-On is therefore the ability to guarantee high-current 
charge/discharge behavior and safe system operation under a defined transient and 
backup envelope—not merely assembling cells into a metal pack. Lite-On’s rack-level 
solution, for example, emphasizes DC-coupled backup, PSU–BBU firmware coordination 
and multilayer battery protection. Panasonic’s own cell-to-module and system 
capabilities also mean that the division of value between battery suppliers and power-
system integrators varies by customer. 
Both Delta and Lite-On can benefit when BBUs remain within IT racks or dedicated 
power racks. Delta has a broader route to follow storage further upstream, given its 
established UPS portfolio and energy-storage systems integrating power conversion, 
batteries and controls. We therefore view Delta as better positioned to pursue pooled-
storage opportunities, but not automatically insulated from lost BBU revenue: capturing 
the replacement system still requires customer wins and competitive execution. 
Lite-On’s demonstrated strengths are more concentrated in rack-level conversion, 
coordinated BBU and 800V power racks. We consequently see greater architecture 
sensitivity if customers move substantial battery content beyond the power rack into 
separately procured facility storage. It could retain conversion, controls and local 
buffering content, but recapturing the displaced battery dollars would require additional 
system participation or partnerships. The distinction is therefore broader upstream 
opportunity for Delta versus greater exposure to rack/power-rack storage for Lite-On—
not an automatic winner and loser from LFP adoption. 
In our model, total power-electronics content rises from approximately US$19k per 
Hopper rack to US$66k for GB200 and US$96k for GB300, driven by higher rack power, 
larger shared power shelves, rack busbars, management electronics and optional 
storage. By Vera Rubin, our integrated 48/54V cases reach approximately US$169k for 
VR200 and US$184k for VR300.  A shift to more pooled memory and lower rack-level 
attachment would not mean lower storage demand across the entire data center, but it 
can reduce our defined rack-and-power-rack TAM.

Stage 3: The 800V power rack is likely the most content-
additive transition
Once rack demand reaches several hundred kilowatts, the constraint is no longer only 
the capacity of individual PSUs. The combination of low-voltage current, copper, 
connectors, airflow and rack space becomes the binding limitation. At 1MW, a 50V 
architecture would carry approximately 20,000A, compared with approximately 1,250A 
at 800V. Moving to 800V therefore reduces current by roughly an order of magnitude 
and allows much more power to be delivered through a manageable number of cables 
and busbars. Delta at Semicon Taiwan 2026 showed how a busbar that carries the 
power through a rack at 54V would need to be 518mm thick and weigh 511kg. At 
800V, the busbar width compresses to 35mm and weight to 35kg. 

The initial 800V architecture is likely to be a localized in-row power rack or sidecar that is 
deliberately evolutionary. Existing 415/480VAC infrastructure feeds the power rack 
sidecar which converts and distributes the power 800VDC. The IT rack can then step 
800V back down to 48/54V and retain much of the existing IBC and VRM architecture. 
That is important for both adoption and content. It avoids requiring the industry to 
redesign the entire rack and node power chain simultaneously, but it also means the 
initial 800V transition adds a new high-voltage layer before eliminating the old low-
voltage one. NVIDIA describes this as a transitional retrofit architecture: it is not the most 
efficient ultimate design because it retains additional conversion equipment, but it 
enables 800V compute racks to operate within existing AC data halls. Schneider similarly 
views rack-level conversion as the most practical initial deployment because it can retain 
conventional upstream AC UPS and limit early fault or protection issues to a smaller 
zone. 
 A typical 800V power rack contains modular AC/DC power shelves, rectifier modules, 
DC PDUs, busbars, cables, contactors, fuses, pre-charge circuitry, isolation and 
monitoring, together with optional BBU or CBU capacity. Delta’s announced 660kW in-
row system for NVIDIA for example uses six 110kW shelves and target up to 98% power 
efficiency. In the BBU configuration, six active shelves deliver 660kW of power and 
integrate 24x20kW BBU modules or 480kW of back-up power. The non-BBU 
configuration instead uses 8 power shelves in a 6 + 2 arrangement, adding 6 active 
shelves and 2 redundant shelves with 12 additional PSU modules. Thus the same 660kW 
rated output and vary on PSU vs. BBU content depending on the required resilience.

The IT rack also gains important new content. Transitional systems may convert 800V to 
48/54V and then to 12V, while the native NVIDIA direction is to move high-ratio 800V-
to-12V conversion close to the GPU, eliminating intermediate conversion stages before 
the final VRM. NVIDIA estimates that direct conversion can improve efficiency and 
reduce the area required near the GPU versus a multi-stage power tree. The architecture 
has another underappreciated advantage: removing conversion and storage hardware 
from the IT rack frees scarce U-space, thermal headroom and servicing access for 
revenue-generating compute. The economic benefit therefore extends beyond power-
system efficiency itself.
From an investment perspective, the initial 800V power-rack transition may be the most 
content-rich part of the transition. The architecture temporarily adds high-voltage 
rectification, protection and distribution while retaining substantial downstream DC/DC 
and POL content in the IT rack.

Key assumptions varying content include installed vs. usable rectifier capacity after 
redundancy, how many IT racks or how much IT load each power racks support, BBU 
and CBU attachment, percent of power backed up, hold-up duration and DC-DC 
conversion in the rack, which will start as a transitional 800V to 54V to 12V conversion 
requiring additional DC-DC shelves before later moving  directly to 800V through a 
busbar to the compute boards for 800V to 12V conversion. 
Our bottom-up work suggests the initial 800V transition is content additive without 
requiring a large increase in value per watt. Across our Vera Rubin sidecar cases, 
modeled rack-to-chip power content is approximately US$0.84–0.85/W, versus roughly 
US$0.68–0.71/W for the preceding integrated 48/54V architecture. The increase reflects 
the addition of a dedicated 800V power rack—including rectification, high-voltage 
distribution and protection and probability-weighted energy storage—while the IT rack 
initially retains substantial DC/DC, distribution and POL content. Absolute dollar content 
therefore scales rapidly with rack power: our model increases from approximately US
$192k for a 227kW VR200 system to approximately US$469k for a 550kW 
configuration, despite relatively stable content intensity within the 800V architecture.
Native 800V changes the mix rather than eliminating the opportunity. As the 54V layer is 
removed, some low-voltage busbar and intermediate conversion content can decline, 
but value migrates toward higher-ratio DC/DC conversion, 800V protection and 
increasingly dense point-of-load power delivery. Our modeled 1.2MW Feynman power-
rack architecture therefore remains near US$0.89/W of rack-to-chip power content. A 
subsequent facility-level SST architecture could lift modelled content further—to 
approximately US$1.21/W in our current case—as medium-voltage transformation and 
rectification shift from conventional magnetic equipment toward semiconductor-rich 
power conversion. These estimates remain architecture dependent, but importantly our 
TAM assumes rising system power and changing content location rather than simply 
extrapolating higher PSU prices.

The transition to higher-voltage DC is unlikely to follow a single architecture across every 
hyperscaler. Our checks suggest AWS may retain a ~50V power-rack architecture for 
Trainium 3 as an interim step, while Google and Meta are considering an earlier move to 
bipolar ±400VDC with 30% penetration of their 2027 racks shifting to this architecture. 
Importantly, ±400VDC is not simply a “lower-voltage” alternative to 800V: the positive 
and negative rails are 800V apart, allowing a balanced system to capture broadly similar 
current and copper benefits while limiting each conductor to roughly 400V relative to 
the midpoint/reference. 
Google’s Mt. Diablo work with Meta and Microsoft explicitly targets ±400VDC delivery 
from a disaggregated sidecar supporting high-density IT racks up to 1MW, with the 
ability to leverage the established 400V EV supply chain an additional potential 
advantage. Vertiv's presentation of Mt. Diablo further illustrates the breadth of the 
sidecar architecture, combining power conversion, distribution, and BBU/CBU storage in 
alternative power-rack configurations. This supports our view that externalizing bulk 
conversion can relocate energy storage into the power rack rather than eliminate it.  We 
would also point out OCP identifies a future Mt. Diablo 2.0 specification supporting 
native 800V as indicator the ±400V is an evolutionary path to 800V. 
From a content perspective, our checks with Delta suggest ±400V and single-bus 800V 
should carry broadly similar power-rack BOM per kW. Both require high-power AC/DC 
rectification, HVDC distribution, optional BBU/CBU storage, busbars and cabling, 
contactors, fuses, pre-charge, sensing and controls, rack-entry protection and 
downstream high-ratio DC/DC conversion.  Delta’s newly demonstrated 840kW ±400V 

in-row rack shown at Semicon Taiwan provides a useful real-world example: five 180kW 
power shelves provide 900kW of installed conversion capacity versus an 840kW system 
rating, with Delta citing N+2 redundancy and battery charging, while BBU or CBU 
storage can be configured separately.   Delta's discussion at Semicon Taiwan of a 
900kW-class installed power architecture and Mt Diablo's support for up to 
1MW power racks also supports our view that ASIC rack power density can rise 
materially over the coming years, expanding the addressable power 
opportunity and increasing the relevance of dedicated side cars. 
The main differences are topology, grounding and component mix rather than a 
fundamentally different architecture or amount of power-electronics content. Bipolar 
±400V introduces a midpoint management and protection of both poles, while allowing 
portions of the design to leverage established 400V EV component ecosystem. 
However, an 800V rail-to-rail voltage does not make ±400VDC and 0-800V supplies 
interchangeable: Vertiv at OCP Asia cautioned that some future IT loads may require the 
move to 800V.  A single 800V bus is electrically simpler but can require higher-voltage 
switching, insulation and fault-interruption capability. We expect broadly similar 
functional power-system content per kW across the approaches, with differences 
concentrated in semiconductor voltage class, protection architecture and component 
count rather than a materially different total BOM.

voltage DC because it still steps the 800V supply back to 48/54V inside the compute 
rack. Longer term, high-voltage DC can be carried deeper into the rack and increasingly 

to the compute node before a high-ratio conversion close to the accelerator. NVIDIA’s 
planned reference design for native 800V illustrates this direction, distributing 800V to 
individual compute nodes where a high-ratio converter steps directly toward the 12V 
intermediate rail. This removes the 48/54V busbar and one layer of intermediate 
conversion, reducing space, copper and conversion losses close to the accelerator.
For the supply chain, this changes the mix rather than eliminating power-electronics 
value. The 800V-to-54V shelf and some low-voltage distribution hardware can 
disappear, but they are replaced by technically more demanding high-ratio DC/DC 
conversion requiring higher-voltage power semiconductors, magnetics, isolation, 
protection and thermal management. We therefore expect value to migrate from 
relatively standardized intermediate conversion toward higher-value node-level 
conversion rather than disappear one-for-one. And regardless of whether the rack 
backbone is 54V, ±400V or 800VDC, the processor ultimately still requires sub-1V rails at 
extremely high current and transient performance, supporting continued growth in POL/
VRM content.
Stage 4: Facility-level 800V moves front-end conversion into 
the grey space
As 800V busways, protection equipment, standards and operating practices mature, 
AC/DC conversion can move farther upstream from the localized sidecar into the grey 
space of the data center. The first step discussed by NVIDIA and shown at the June 
Computex show in 2026 by Vertiv is likely to be a low-voltage power center that 
aggregates 400–480VAC input and supplies 800VDC to multiple racks or rows. Longer 
term, transformer-rectifier units, medium-voltage rectifiers or solid-state transformers 
can convert 13.8kV or 34.5kV power directly into 800VDC, reducing or eliminating parts 
of the conventional 480VAC layer. 
Figure 37: 800 VDC infrastructure roadmap: power conversion scales from rack side cars to multi-MW facility blocks
Source: UBS, NVIDIA, Schneider
NVIDIA describes approximately 1.5MVA low-voltage rectifier strings that can be 
paralleled on a common DC bus, while medium-voltage rectifier and SST concepts can 
reach several megawatts per unit. Schneider’s roadmap similarly progresses from a 

roughly 660kW–1.2MW localized sidecar to 2.4–4.8MW power centers and ultimately 
5–10MW facility power blocks. These figures are illustrative rather than fixed industry 
standards, but they show how the unit of deployment is shifting rapidly from the rack 
toward the multi-MW power block. 
Figure 38: Power content migrates from rack-level conversion to multi-MW facility systems
Localized 800V sidecar Centralized LV power center MV rectifier / SST power block
Location Beside IT rack Row / data hall Facility
Input 415/480VAC 400–480VAC 13.8/34.5kVAC
Output 800VDC 800VDC busway 800VDC busway
AC-DC Rectification scale 0.66–1.2MW 2.4–4.8MW 5–10MW
Conversion hardware Modular AC/DC shelves Pooled LV rectifiers TRU, MV rectifier or SST
Storage Optional local BBU/CBU Central DC UPS / storage Facility BESS + local fast storage
Distribution Rack cable Row/data-hall busway Facility DC network
Content implication Highest rack-level content Pooling and larger DC PDU Large engineered power block
Unit of sale US$/rack US$/MW US$/power block
Source: UBS, Schneider, NVIDIA
A medium-voltage rectifier or transformer-rectifier unit is likely to be the more mature 
near-term solution because similar systems already operate in industrial applications. 
SSTs offer the longer-term potential to combine voltage transformation, rectification 
and active controls in a more compact architecture, but multi-MW power-module 
reliability, thermal management and protection remain development challenges. 
The result is not that power-electronics content disappears. Rather, the unit of sale and 
location of value change:
 Rack-level rectifier modules and some BBU capacity can be pooled.
 Row/facility DC switchboards, busways and PDUs become larger.
 DC breakers, contactors, isolation, metering and protection coordination become 
more important.
 Energy storage can be aggregated into a centralized DC UPS or BESS.
 Software, controls, commissioning and service become more valuable.
 The IT rack still requires rack-entry protection, high-ratio DC/DC and VRM/VPD 
close to the xPU.
This shifts the opportunity from a relatively standardized PSU sale toward a multi-MW 
engineered system. It should favor suppliers with broad power-conversion portfolios, 
facility-integration capabilities, protection expertise, controls and field-service 
infrastructure.
Energy storage also becomes increasingly layered. Capacitors close to compute handle 
the fastest workload changes; rack- or row-level BBU/DC UPS supports short-duration 
ride-through; and facility BESS manages longer load averaging, source transfer and grid 
requirements. We therefore expect greater total storage and control content per MW, 
but rack-level BBU unit penetration could ultimately plateau or decline if storage 
becomes pooled upstream. 
AI power TAM: US$91bn by 2030, built bottom-up 
from chips, racks, watts and power BOM
We estimate the AI server power-electronics TAM rises from US$6.6bn in 2025 to US
$91.1bn in 2030, a 69% CAGR, with approximately US$285bn of cumulative power-
system content over 2025–30. We build up the power TAM opportunity platform by 
platform leveraging our bottom-up accelerator shipment assumptions from 
UBS CoWoS/HBM build assumptions for ASICs and UBS GPU unit model pulling in our 
coverage assumptions on AMD and NVIDIA AI GPU shipments.  We convert our chip 
units to racks and build up TDP at the chip and rack level for announced systems with 
higher visibility through 2027. Beyond 2027, we extend the model using industry 
feedback on the expected scale-up of systems at the chip, rack and power level, while 

tapering deployment growth to reflect increasingly binding power and capex constraints 
and a normalization toward underlying hyperscaler cash-flow growth. 
Our model combines two bottom-up builds: accelerator units are translated into rack 
deployments and supported IT watts, while architecture-specific component BOMs 
determine power-system content per supported IT watt. These two analyses converge in 
our annual TAM estimate. 
For each NVIDIA, AMD and custom-ASIC platform, we forecast accelerator units, 
convert these to racks using the number of accelerators per system, and estimate rack/
system IT power using package TDP and platform-level power assumptions. We then 
then construct the associated power-electronics BOM including PSUs/shelves/controls, 
battery or capacitor storage, HVDC conversion/distribution, downstream DC/DC and 
rack-power infrastructure, and normalize the resulting content to the IT watts 
supported.   Our assumptions incorporate TDP , redundancy, BBU/CBU attach rates and 
architecture-specific changes in content as power electronics migrate from the IT rack 
into a separate power rack or side car and initially add additional DC-DC distribution 
content. 
Figure 39: ASIC TDPs per rack (kW)
Source: UBS estimates
Where conversion, backup power or distribution remains integrated within the IT rack, 
that content is included directly in the rack BOM; where it migrates into a separate 
power rack or sidecar, we allocate the external power-rack content back across the IT 
load it supports. This allows us to compare architectures on a consistent US$/IT watt 
basis regardless of where the physical equipment resides.
The result is a TAM driven by three distinct variables rather than one heroic assumption: 
rack volume, watts per rack and power content per watt. Between 2025 and 2030, we 
estimate AI server rack shipments grow at only a 12% CAGR, while blended rack/system 
IT power rises at a 39% CAGR. Together, these drive annual AI IT capacity deployed at a 
55% CAGR. Blended power-system content per watt adds a further 9% CAGR, 
resulting in a 69% power-TAM CAGR. Put differently, growth in IT GW deployed driven 
increasingly by rising rack power density rather than physical rack unit growth is the 
dominant TAM multiplier, with higher power content per watt providing an additional 
boost.

Source: UBS
We start with accelerator units, not rack shipments

A key input in our model is our existing bottom-up accelerator forecast leveraging 
memory, foundry, back-end, fabless/design service and ODM supply inputs. As detailed 
in Figure 15U B S  p r o j e c t i o n s  f o r  A I  a c c e l e r a t o r  s h i p m e n t s :  + 3 9 %  c o m p u t e  d i e  u n i t  C A G R, we forecast bottom-up accelerator shipment forecasts across NVIDIA and 
AMD GPUs and the major custom-ASIC platforms, including AWS, Google, Meta, 
Microsoft, and OpenAI.  We then apply a deployment-lag assumption under which 
75% of each year's accelerator output enters rack builds in the same calendar year and 
25% in the following year, reflecting system-assembly and supply-chain lead times. We 
align the associated rack power and power-system BOM with the same deployment 
cohort.
We separately model other rack types where required by the architecture. For example, a 
platform may place CPUs, scale-up components or power electronics in adjacent racks 
rather than in the main accelerator rack. The objective is not simply to count cabinets, 
but to determine how much IT load and associated power-system hardware is required 
to support the deployed accelerator base.
This bottom-up approach produces total AI server rack deployments of approximately 
rising from 208k in 2025, 297k in 2026, 428k in 2027, 397k in 2028, 342k in 2029 and 
369k in 2030. The non-linear trajectory is important: physical rack units actually decline 
in several years even while power TAM continues to rise sharply.
Figure 41: AI rack units deployments peak in 2027, while rising power density sustains IT GW growth 
Source: UBS
Rack power converts rack deployments into IT GW - the dominant 
volume driver of the TAM
We translate physical rack systems into IT watts based on accelerator package TDP , 
accelerator count per rack, expected system-level power and other IT loads required by 
the platform, including CPUs, memory, networking and rack-level electronics where 
appropriate. This distinction becomes increasingly important as power density rises. Our 
blended AI server rack/system IT power increases from approximately 55kW in 2025 to 
89kW in 2026, 119kW in 2027, 171kW in 2028, 257kW in 2029 and 283kW in 2030. 
Within this average there is considerable dispersion: our GPU-system average reaches 
approximately 401kW by 2030, while the ASIC average is approximately 204kW, 
although we could see upside to that projection as new announced compute dense 
systems are announced in the out years of the forecast period. 

Figure 42: 358GW cumulative gross deployments over 2024-30 (401GW of electricity at PUE 1.12) 
Source: UBS
Multiplying rack volume by rack/system IT power derives annual IT capacity deployed, a 
more relevant measure of the opportunity than rack units alone. We estimate this rises 
from 11.5GW in 2025 to 26.5GW in 2026, 50.8GW in 2027, 67.7GW in 2028, 87.9GW 
in 2029 and 104.5GW in 2030, a 55% CAGR.
This is why we believe rack-unit forecasts alone increasingly understate the AI power 
opportunity. In 2028, for example, we model rack shipments declining approximately 
7%, yet AI IT capacity rises roughly 33%. In 2029, rack units decline another 
approximately 14%, but IT capacity still increases approximately 30%. The industry is 
deploying fewer incremental cabinets in those years, but considerably more watts.
We separately calculate facility power at a 1.12 PUE for data-center infrastructure 
context. Importantly, we do not apply PUE to inflate the rack power-electronics TAM; the 
content model is normalized to IT-side watts. IT GW represents the rated IT power 
associated with our modelled annual hardware deployments, rather than average 
electricity consumption. Cumulative deployments are shown before retirements and 
replacements at 358.4GW from 2024-2030; facility power at 1.12 is presented 
separately at 401.4GW.  
We build the power BOM architecture by architecture
We construct a bottom-up power BOM for each major architecture. The physical 
location of that content changes considerably over time. In Hopper and early Blackwell 
systems, much of the conversion and distribution hardware sits directly in the IT rack. As 
rack power rises, BBU capacity, larger power shelves, busbars and higher-capacity 
distribution increase content. Moving toward ±400/800VDC architectures adds a new 
high-voltage distribution layer and increasingly externalizes bulk AC/DC conversion into 
a separate power rack or sidecar. Native high-voltage architectures can subsequently 
simplify some downstream conversion stages, while SST adoption could move still more 
power transformation into the power-electronics opportunity.
We therefore model both the IT rack and any dedicated power rack/sidecar as one 
power system. If a dedicated power rack supports one IT rack, its content is fully 
attributed to that system; if it supports multiple IT racks, its BOM is allocated across the 
supported IT load. This avoids the misleading conclusion that moving a PSU or BBU out 
of the compute rack somehow removes it from the TAM—it changes its physical location 
and sometimes its architecture, but the relevant economic question is the power-system 
content required per IT watt.

Figure 43: Power-system BOM migrates from the IT rack to a dedicated power rack as density rises
Source: UBS
Our detailed BOM contains the individual elements—AC/DC modules, power shelves, 
management and control, BBU and CBU shelves, DC PDUs, high-voltage conversion and 
distribution, busbars, rack-entry hardware, point-of-load conversion and, where 
applicable, SST. We roll these into six buckets: PSUs/shelves/controls; backup power and 
energy storage; HVDC conversion/distribution; downstream DC/DC power electronics; 
rack power infrastructure; and SST/upstream power transformation.
Content does not just increase—the mix changes materially across 
generations
Our NVIDIA architecture build provides a useful illustration. We estimate rack-plus-
sidecar power content increases from approximately US$19k for Hopper/H200 to US
$67k for GB200 and US$96k for GB300, before rising to approximately US$170k for 
VR200, US$233k for our VR300 Oberon configuration and US$1.07mn for RF200. An 
RF200 configuration incorporating upstream SST increases modeled power-system 
content to approximately US$1.45mn.
On a content/watt basis, our estimated power content rises from approximately US
$0.42/W for Hopper to US$0.56/W for GB200, US$0.68/W for GB300, US$0.85/W for 
VR200, US$0.93/W for VR300 Oberon, and US$0.89/W for RF200. Our SST-equipped 
RF200 scenario reaches approximately US$1.45/W, although we treat SST penetration 
separately rather than assuming it across all deployments.

falling PSU dollars. PSU, shelf and control content rises materially in absolute terms 
through most generations, but its share declines because new content pools are being 
layered around it. Backup power, HVDC distribution, larger busbars and rack 
infrastructure all become increasingly meaningful as the architecture transitions. If SST 
becomes part of the ultimate deployment architecture, upstream transformation 
represents a further potential content pool rather than simply another larger PSU.

Our bottom-up platform model allows us to isolate two of the largest individual power-
content pools: front-end power supply content and rack-level energy storage. We 
estimate AI server PSU & distribution TAM (rises from approximately US$3.6bn in 2025 
to US$41.5bn in 2030, a 63% CAGR, as rapidly rising IT GW is compounded by larger 
power modules, higher-capacity shelves and richer controls). The content in our build-up 
includes the PSU, shelf and controls, power management controller and HVDC 
conversion (±400V/800V to 54/48V shelves).   This component is the largest component 
of the white space power electronics stack, although its share of total power TAM 
declines from approximately 55% in 2025 to 46% in 2030 as new content pools in 
storage, protection, and eventually upstream transformation grow faster around it.
We estimate rack- and power-rack energy-storage TAM across BBU and CBU rises from 
approximately US$0.8bn in 2025 to US$15.9bn in 2030, an 82% CAGR, with modelled 
content increasing from approximately US$0.06 to US$0.14 per IT watt and from 12% 
to 17% of total power TAM as attach rates increase for hyperscale data centers and 
ASICs grow faster vs. GPU servers. The mix between battery and capacitive storage 
remains architecture-dependent: BBUs provide longer ride-through, while CBUs address 
higher-frequency transient and load-smoothing requirements, and some systems may 
incorporate both. Longer term, greater pooling of battery capacity into centralized UPS/
BESS could reduce rack-level BBU attachment without eliminating the need for fast local 
buffering. Our US$15.9bn estimate therefore captures modeled BBU/CBU within the IT 
rack and power rack, but excludes centralized facility-level storage.

APAC Focus: AI Power—From watts to gigawatts
AI power is emerging as the next constraint on compute—grid availability and
hyperscale cash flows could moderate growth later this decade, even as rising
power density creates a larger power-electronics content opportunity than chip and
rack counts imply. Our bottom-up model estimates a 69% CAGR to US$91.1bn AI
server power TAM from 2025-2030, front-end loaded with rising content/watt
sustaining growth. Our bottom-up rack and power model converts UBS accelerator
forecasts into racks, IT GW and architecture-specific BOMs across major GPU and
customer ASIC platforms. The shift from integrated power supply units (PSUs)
toward dedicated power racks, 400/800V distribution and ultimately solid-state
transformers (SST) expands content per watt and creates opportunities across
power supply, energy storage, MLCCs and power semis.
Strong growth in 2027E precedes the 400/800V transition
While the market has focused on slower migration to 800VDC, our bottom-up rack and
power model points to growth in deployed compute GW and architectural upgrades at
the chip, rack and grid level driving content gains before widespread high-voltage
adoption. We see a strong 2027 driven by +65% YoY accelerator die growth, Rubin's
~60% higher rack power and AMD's move to rack-scale systems. 400V/800V becomes
a larger driver in 2028-29 as rising power density outgrows low-voltage distribution.
Grid constraints moderate 2028-30E; rising content/watt sustains power TAM
We project +12% CAGR in AI rack units and  +39% CAGR in TDP (thermal design
power) per rack, driving +55% CAGR in IT capacity deployed. We taper 2028-30
growth for potential grid, capex and cash-flow constraints, anchoring our TAM to
deployable IT GW, slowing growth to 44%/37%/20% in 2028-30.  Against that
moderation, power system content rises at a +9% CAGR from US$0.57 to US$0.87/W,
lifting our AI power TAM to US$91bn by 2030. Dedicated 660kW-1.2MW power racks
add PSU density, DC-DC distribution, energy storage, busbars, protection, and controls.
Rising deployed GW & richer content support the chain even as constraints rise
We expect growth  in GW compute plus architecture upgrades to lift content across the
power chain. We see Buy-rated Delta and Lite-On as the two direct beneficiaries: Delta's
broad grid-to-chip porfolio helps sustain its ~40% share of a rising TAM while Lite-On is
expanding customer qualifications and ramping ASIC platforms. Rising AI power also
supports strong pricing/tight supply for MLCCs (Murata/TDK/Semco) and near rack and
pooled energy storage (Panasonic/Samsung SDI). In power semis, we prefer Buy-rated
TI, ADI and STM, where power offers  upside potential, over Infineon (Neutral).

Executive summary
AI compute growth increasingly a power-density story
The rapid growth of AI compute is driving higher power density at every level of the
system.  Power per GPU accelerator increases from ~700W for NVIDIA's Hopper  to 1.3-
1.4kW for Blackwell and 2.3kW for Vera Rubin.  More accelerators are also integrated
into each chip, moving up from 1 die on Hopper to 2 dies with Blackwell and upcoming
ASICs in late 2027 will push 4 per package. With scale-up bandwidth 18x faster than
scale out and more optimal for dense training and inference clusters, rack compute
density continues to rise, taking accelerator dies per rack from 32 on Hopper to 144 on
Blackwell and future architectures could scale to 576+. Rack power consequently rises
from ~40–50kW for Hopper to 140kW for GB300, 227kW for VR200 and 500-1,000kW
+ for Feynman and beyond. To support that power density, we see AI power upgrading
from a relatively standardized PSU market into a critical grid-to-chip system spanning
conversion, storage, distribution, protection, controls and cooling.
Deployable IT GW reflecting power constraints helps shape the out-
year TAM
We introduce a bottom-up AI GPU and ASIC hardware rack and power TAM based on
accelerator units by platform, accelerators per rack, rack configuration and TDP per rack,
ultimately translating these assumptions into annual IT GW deployed. We taper 2028-
30 growth for potential grid, permitting, capex and cash-flow constraints, anchoring the
out-year TAM slowing to 44%/37%/20% in 2028-30 to deployable IT GW.  Against that
moderation, our bottom-up assumptions imply AI rack units grow only ~12% CAGR
over 2025–30E, but average rack TDP rises 39%, lifting annual IT capacity deployed at a
55% CAGR to 104.5GW in 2030. Across NVIDIA, AMD and ASICs—most notably TPU
and Trainium—we model roughly 340GW of incremental AI IT capacity over 2026–30,
equivalent to approximately 380GW of associated data-center capacity at a 1.12 PUE.
Capacity plans require further work on grid and behind-the-meter
power
UBS Evidence Lab tracks approximately 201GW of global data-center capacity under
construction or planned, including ~126GW in the US. If the US represents 55–60% of
incremental capacity, the gap requires improvement in permitting, grid interconnection,
generation, construction and financing. UBS US Utilities identifies potential upside from
higher plant completion rates, inclusion of early-stage projects not yet in the approval/
construction pipeline and fewer retirements than in its base case. Separately, UBS
Americas Sustainability (link) estimates ~133GW of additional usable capacity from
energy sources beyond traditional grid transmission in its base case, rising to ~156GW
under a full-absorption scenario. These include batteries/peak shaving, gas generation,
utility-scale solar, fuel cells and solar-plus-storage, providing potential pathways to
support a meaningful portion of the incremental capacity required by our accelerator
assumptions, subject to timing, permitting and execution.
We therefore taper deployment growth in 2028–30 as grid capacity, permitting, capex
and cash-flow constraints increasingly factor into investment decisions and deployment
timing. We view 2026–27 primarily as a volume and power-density phase, while
deployability and power architecture become increasingly important determinants of
growth from 2028 onward.
The power stack progressively moves outside the IT rack
Even with a more constrained GW deployment curve, the power-electronics opportunity
can continue to expand because each deployed watt becomes more content-rich as rack
density rises. The same physical constraints that ultimately limit deployment including
current, copper, rack space, thermal loss and resilience also force the power architecture
to evolve toward larger shared systems, higher distribution voltages and more efficient
architectures.
Our industry feedback points to an upcoming power transition in four overlapping
stages: 1) AC power distributes to the IT rack where server PSUs (power supply
units) and power shelves convert it into 48/54VDC and further down to <1V to power

the accelerator. 2) Higher-density rack systems centralize PSUs, power shelves and
energy storage (BBU  (battery back-up units)/CBU (capacitor back-up units) at the rack
level and increasingly move them into a separate power rack. 3) 800V or ±400V sidecars
convert and distribute power at higher voltage before stepping it down close to the
compute rack. 4) Greenfield facilities can centralize conversion at the row or facility
level, ultimately using medium-voltage rectification or SST to deliver native 800VDC
across the data hall. The migration path adds value increasing amount of power
conversion, distribution, storage, and protection moving upstream, while the final DC/
DC conversion remains close to the accelerator.
The physical rationale is compelling. Delivering a 227kW rack at 54V requires more than
4,000A. Moving distribution to 800V reduces current by approximately 15x and
theoretical resistive loss in the same conductor by more than 200x, reducing copper,
losses and thermal stress. We estimate that more advanced grid-to-chip configurations
could improve overall efficiency from roughly 82% to 87%, saving approximately 60–
70MW of input power for each 1GW of IT load.Importantly, NVIDIA may initially extend
48/54V farther while Google and Meta appear positioned to introduce +/- 400V
architectures earlier alongside Amazon 48V power rack for some Trainium 3 systems
and 800V for Trainium 4. We therefore see 2027-28 as an overlap period across multiple
power architectures rather than a single industry wide switchover - one reason our
strong 2027 TAM does not depend on strong 800V adoption.

Power content grows faster than rack TDP
Our platform BOM analysis indicates that rack power content increases close to tenfold
from Hopper through VR300, versus approximately sixfold growth in rack TDP (thermal
design power). Indicative content rises from roughly US$19,000 per Hopper rack to US
$67,000 for GB200, US$96,000 for GB300, US$170,000 for VR200 and US$183,000
for VR300. Content intensity increases from approximately US$0.42/W to US$0.73/W
across these platforms and reaches a blended US$0.87/W in our 2030 market model.
The content increase extends well beyond adding more PSUs. PSU modules scale from
approximately 5.5kW toward 12–18kW, shelves increase from roughly 33kW to 72–
110kW, and dedicated power racks reach 660–840kW. BBU/CBU, busbars, DC/DC
conversion, power distribution, protection, controls and liquid cooling all expand.

Transitional 400/800V architectures should be particularly content-rich because they add
high-voltage power racks, distribution and protection before existing AC and 48/55V
conversion chain is eliminated. Native 800V and SST may later remove some mature
stages, but shift value into higher-power rectification, storage, protection, wide-
bandgap semiconductors and controls rather than disappearing.
Our bottom-up AI power TAM reaches US$91.1bn in 2030
We calculate TAM by applying architecture-specific power content per IT watt to annual
AI IT capacity deployed. This drives our AI server power TAM from US$6.6bn in 2025 to
US$17.7bn in 2026, US$38.2bn in 2027, US$55.1bn in 2028 and US$91.1bn in 2030E,
a 69% CAGR and US$285bn of cumulative TAM over 2025-30E. Importantly, the near-
term ramp does not depend on broad 800V adoption. Higher accelerator volumes, rising
rack TDP , larger PSUs and shelves, and greater BBU/CBU content already drive
substantial growth under conventional 48/54V architectures. The move to power racks
and 800V becomes a larger incremental contributor from 2028 onward.

2027 growth does not depend on broad 800V; more important for 2028
Our sensitivity work suggests the timing of NVIDIA’s initial 800V power-rack ramp has a
relatively modest impact on the overall 2027 TAM: each 10ppt change in NVIDIA power-
rack penetration moves our total TAM by only ~1%. The larger drivers for 2027 are the
sharp increase in deployed IT GW (+92% YoY), Rubin’s higher system power (+60%),
AMD’s move toward rack-scale systems and early power-rack adoption across the top
custom ASIC platforms. By 2028, architecture becomes a larger driver as Google/
Amazon should ramp power racks with chip and rack TDP rising with their shift to 4 die
chip architectures to offset milder ramp with Rubin Ultra's similar Oberon and mild
TDP upgrade before a steeper ramp toward native 800V systems into the Feynman
generation also likely shifting to a 4 die architecture and 288+ GPUs/rack. We therefore
see 2026–27 primarily as a watts-growth phase, followed by a stronger architecture/
content-per-watt phase from 2028 onward.
ASICs broaden the power-rack transition and nearly match GPU power
TAM by 2030
NVIDIA remains the largest individual platform, with US$41.8bn of modeled 2030
power TAM, but it is no longer the industry’s only meaningful driver. We estimate total
GPU-related power TAM of US$49.2bn in 2030, or 54% of the market, versus US
$42.0bn, or 46%, from custom ASIC systems. Google, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft/
OpenAI and other ASIC deployments therefore become almost as important as NVIDIA
and AMD combined.
This mix also argues against assuming one universal power architecture. NVIDIA is
leading the move toward 800VDC, while hyperscalers may continue using 48/50/54V,
±400V or localized 800V designs for different periods. Rack structure, CPU separation,
redundancy and storage requirements also vary. Suppliers must qualify across multiple
platforms and support several architectures simultaneously, increasing the value of
engineering breadth and customer relationships.

Deployments determine TAM; architecture determines who captures it
Deployed IT GW is the largest sensitivity in our model: a 10% change in 2030 capacity
changes TAM by approximately US$9.1bn. A US$0.05/W change in blended content
changes TAM by approximately US$5.2bn. An additional 1GW in 2027 adds
approximately 4.2 percentage points to TAM growth, while an additional US$0.01/W of
content adds approximately 2.9 percentage points. This reinforces our view that the
magnitude and timing of AI hardware deployments remain the most important variables
for the 2026–27 inflection; widespread native 800V adoption is not required for a strong
2027 outcome.  The timing of 800V and SST has a larger effect on revenue mix and
supplier positioning than on the underlying power requirement. A one-year delay in
800V shifts content toward conventional PSUs, 48/54V shelves and localized DC/DC
rather than eliminating demand. Faster adoption benefits suppliers qualified in HVDC
power racks, storage, protection and high-ratio conversion. This distinction also reduces
the dependence of our 2026–27 TAM on precise forecasts of the 800V roadmap.

White-space and grey-space competitors converge
The transition blurs the historical separation between white-space suppliers of IT rack
power and grey-space suppliers of UPS, switchgear, transformers and facility
distribution. White-space leaders are moving upstream into power racks, HVDC and SST,
while Vertiv, Schneider and Eaton are extending facility-level capabilities closer to the
compute rack. Flex competes through manufacturing and system integration, while
Advanced Energy, AcBel and Megmeet are relevant in select platforms.
As power domains expand from standalone PSU modules to hundreds-of-kW power
racks and eventually multi-MW systems, value shifts toward engineered power systems.
This favors suppliers with platform qualification, high-density engineering, breadth
across conversion, storage, distribution, protection and cooling, and the ability to
integrate and service systems globally. These requirements should slow commoditization
despite increasing Chinese competition. Power and infrastructure related revenue across

our selected vendor reporting categories rises from US$56bn in 2024 to US$196bn in
2030E. Although the reporting scopes are not directly comparable, this illustrates the
scale, opportunity and investment required to compete.
Supply chain implications: Power, storage, and MLCC beneficiaries
We would highlight several areas benefiting from the architecture upgrades
supplementing a grid constrained moderation in IT GW of capacity deployed.
 Power supply and storage are the most direct beneficiaries. Our preferred
power names are Delta and Lite-On: Delta has the broadest grid-to-chip
exposure and ~39–43% share of a rising AI power TAM, while Lite-On (also
initiating with a Buy and NT$400 target) with improving execution, customer
penetration and power rack ramps to lift sales and margins. We forecast their
relevant revenues rising from US$3.0bn/US$3.0bn in 2026 to US$11.0bn/US
$11.0bn in 2030, respectively.  We also view potential for Megmeet (Neutral) in
China to outgrow from a low base with fast development to gain qualifications
and customer responsiveness to secure new design-ins.
 Global infrastructure vendors can extend toward the white space. Vertiv,
Schneider and Eaton bring established positions in UPS, distribution, switchgear,
controls, and cooling, giving them a natural path into higher-voltage, rack-
adjacent power as AI architectures scale. Vertiv is particularly well positioned
where power and cooling converge, while Schneider and Eaton can leverage
broader data-center electrical infrastructure. Relative to Delta and Lite-On,
however, they have less historical content immediately adjacent to the accelerator.
Flex and Advanced Energy (both Not Rated) are more focused on power-
conversion, with Flex combining power, cooling, racks and large scale
manufacturing while Advanced Energy targets high performance convergence.
 Energy storage should also expand as AI power rises. We view energy
storage as a strong growth area with the BBU battery back-up unit (BBU) market
rising from US$2.5bn in 2026 to US$12.8bn by 2030 and including capacitor
back-up unit (CBU) from US$3.1bn to US$15.9bn. We view different architectures
with some positioning back-up power with BBU near-rack but over time moving to
pooled storage. Panasonic appears better positioned in compact cylindrical rack
storage, while Samsung SDI has potential upside from LFP and larger pooled/UPS
applications .
 MLCCs - rising contribution from data center power. We see opportunities as
voltage and power density rise. 800V/SST architectures increase high-voltage
capacitor content, benefiting MLCC suppliers including Murata, TDK and
Semco.  TDK sees its AI-related MLCC business with 30-40% share growing
>100% YoY from a small base.
 AI power semiconductors. We also view AI data-center power semiconductors
as a strong structural growth market, but favor suppliers with capacity and
differentiated new products given the risk that infrastructure availability constrains
deployment. Our preferred exposures include TI gaining share in PSUs/IBCs,
Analog Devices gaining share in VRMs, and STMicro’s photonics exposure
provides additional upside. We are more conservative on Infineon (Neutral) with
high share but also high expectations.

AI power ramping with package power, rack density and
rising GW of deployments
The AI infrastructure build-out is increasing power demand on three levels: 1) rising
power per accelerator package, 2) rising power per rack and 3) increasing the GW of
AI hardware deployed. The rise in power, which is driven by higher compute density is
designed to minimize data movement to save time and energy, driving as much compute
as possible on one die/package then as much as possible in a rack and then once that is
exhausted toward communicate across racks. Every step outward gets slower, consumes
more energy per bit and costs more.
More compute per package drives higher chip power
At the chip level, the accelerate wants access to the largest possible amount of compute
sharing the fastest, closest memory and interconnect and driving a push toward ever
larger chip packages integrating multiple chipsets.  Increasing compute inside an
accelerator gives several advantages: 1) less communication overhead exchanging data
on chip and with nearby HBM and SRAM rather than sending over a networking link,
2) better high bandwidth memory (HBM) utilization maximizing the adjacent compute
to the memory, 3) ability to run more of a model layer rather than inefficiently splitting
across accelerators, and 4) reuse more data locally vs. paying the bandwidth and energy
cost moving it around.
The foundries and advanced packaging manufacturers are enabling these move up to
larger multi-die accelerators by upgrading their advanced packaging to support larger
chipsets. TSMC's CoWoS (chip on wafer on substrate) roadmap has expanded to
multiple reticles and will upgrade further to CoPoS (chip on panel on substrate) in the
next few years migrating from 12" wafer based packaging  to larger 310x310 panels
capable of more efficiently packaging the larger chips. UBS also profiled Intel's EMIB-T
which can scale to 6-8 reticles now and targets over 12 reticles by 2028 (link).

Scale-up economics push more compute and power into
each rack
The same logic for more compute density on chip also applies to the rack to make the
whole server behave like one accelerator and maximize utilization of those accelerators.
AI uses a high degree of parallel compute in training and inference that must require
different GPUs calculating operations to quickly exchange results. The ability to have 72
GPUs or accelerators communicate over a high bandwidth low latency scale-up network
allows greater efficiency than scattered across many independent racks connected by
Ethernet / Infiniband networking.
Communication that remains within the rack generally avoids additional network hops,
optical links and latency associated with crossing rack boundaries. This can improve
accelerator utilization and reduce the amount of time expensive compute sits idle
waiting for data or synchronization. The increase in rack power is not only a by-product
of faster chips. It is partly an economically rational decision to place more of the scale-up

system within a single rack.
The scale-up bandwidth is vastly higher and latency lower making it optimal to keep
communications between accelerators within a rack.  NVIDIA's NVLink scale-up domain
has improved from 900GB/second bidirectional bandwidth between GPUs to 3.6TB/
second from Hopper to Rubin, keeping it at an 18x bandwidth advantage over its scale
out bandwidth between adjacent racks improving from 50GB/second to 200GB/second
over the same time frame.
The speed and latency advantage of scale-up is particularly importance for
communication heavy inference operations including 1) tensor parallelism: splitting a
layer of compute across many GPUs which need to exchange data, 2) MoE (mixture of
experts) parallelism to efficiently route tokens to experts residing on different GPUs,
3) gradients/intermediate results that need to be combined across GPUs, and 4) large
model inference including the weights, activations and KV cache workloads that need to
move data between workloads. For large frontier mixture of expert models, scale-up is
well suited for the frequent token exchange between experts for fast coordination.
Scale-out still has its place connecting hundreds of these racks together for a large
training job to aggregate compute, inference jobs that can be replicated on multiple
racks to serve multiple users, disaggregation of prefill and decode into separate racks
during inference, bulk transfers of data between racks, and computation of batches of
data that can operate in parallel.

Accelerator roadmaps show rising rack compute and power
density
The trends to higher power per chip and per rack are visible across the major
GPU (NVIDIA and AMD) and ASIC accelerators (Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta and
other start-ups) maximizing compute density on each chipset to increase compute
performance at low latency for training and inference. Rack power also grows not only
because each accelerator consumes more power, but also because the rack contains
more of the complete AI system including the accelerator packages, host CPUs and
memory, scale-up switches, scale out network interface cards (NICs) and data processing
units (DPUs), management and storage controllers, liquid cooling pumps and manifolds,
and additional conversion loss and energy buffering.
NVIDIA's GPU accelerators are seeing rise in power per GPU, GPUs per package, GPUs
per rack. Its Hopper generation introduced in 2023 had one large monolithic H100  die  at
700W and 32 GPUs per server rack connected by NVLink networking. While the 32 chips
at 700kW draws about 23kW of power, total TDP (thermal design power) is
45kW including the host CPU, system memory, network adapters, NVLink switch, power
conversion loss and auxiliary components. Blackwell and Blackwell Ultra upgraded the
TDP to 120 and 140kW respectively with each  GPU package upgrading to 2 reticle dies
at 650/700W. Rubin steps up TDP further to 227kW in the Max-P version with each die
moving up to 1,150W.
For Rubin Ultra's planned release in H227, NVIDIA originally pitched to upgrade further
to 4 dies per GPU and 576 dies per rack although we believe has scaled back to using the
same Oberon rack with 72 GPUs and 2 dies per GPU.   We view the scale back a function
of 4 dies being too large to efficiently produce on TSMC's 12" CoWoS until the larger

more efficient CoPoS packaging is commercialized in 2028 and a proposed Kyber rack
architecture with 144 blades and 288/576 dies per rack having complications with the
midplane material, liquid cooling leakage control on the vertical shelves and customer
interest to change rack design.
For AMD, its MI accelerator architecture is also upgrading from MI300 to MI455 from 32
GPUs to 72 GPUs, allowing it to upgrade accelerator chiplets per rack from 256 to 576
and raising the TDP from 40kW to 235kW.   For MI500, a megapod that can connect 256
GPUs is a possible development option that could scale the rack TDP to 1MW.

Google keeps its 64 TPU package per rack configuration but upgrades power per die
and die per package.  The major transition came with TPUv7x moving from 1 to 2
compute dies per package and also doubling power per die to 1.1kW. v8 upcoming in
H226 has a v8i for inference maintaining dual die configuration while v8t has one higher
power compute die optimized for training.  We expect TPU v9 to further push up
performance with higher power dies to raise the rack TDP from 90kW on TPUv8i to
200kW for TPU v9.
Scale-up economics favor higher rack density
Concentrating compute improves floor-space productivity and can reduce the number
and length of external cables. These benefits help explain why AWS is doubling Trainium
rack density and why AMD and NVIDIA are designing complete 72-GPU rack-scale
systems rather than only increasing standalone server performance.
Our central conclusion is that the power trajectory remains structural toward denser
compute and rack configurations supported by the silicon vendor roadmap toward
multi-die systems, TSMC and Intel's roadmap to support multiple reticle packaging with
CoPoS and EMIB_T respectively and rack architectures which are improving the scale-up
bandwidth to allow multiple accelerators to behave as a single unit with lower latency.
The rise in compute density per rack will have positive implications for the
power electronics TAM by increasing the conversion and distribution of power
wattage from the grid to the rack and ultimately the chip. The market has been
concerned about NVIDIA's Kyber delay, as the architecture would have increased the
scale-up density from Oberon's 72 GPU packages per system to 144.  However, power-
density increases do not depend solely on increasing the number of GPU packages per
rack. Density can also rise materially through more compute dies per package,
supported by the advanced packaging roadmap toward larger multi-die systems
including TSMC's CoPoS and Intel's EMIB-T supporting multiple reticle sizes and 4+
large compute dies per package in coming years.
As accelerator platforms expand from two compute dies with Blackwell toward four and
potentially more, even a 72-GPU configuration could support materially higher rack
power density, driving greater requirements for power conversion, distribution and rack
level back-up power. Blackwell was about 3.5 reticle sizes supported by TSMC's
roadmap but by 2027, TSMC can support 14x reticle CoWoS (10 compute dies + 20
HBM stacks), plans to extend it further with 310x310 panels planned for volume by
2028 and as far as system on wafer (SoW-X supporting 40x reticles).

Data center power availability increasingly constrains the

Our supply-chain deployment assumptions are aggressive, but the out-year ramp
ultimately requires sufficient land, power, permitting and data-center infrastructure. Our
modeled 2027-30 AI hardware deployments require approximately 348GW of gross
data-center power capacity at a 1.12 PUE. NVIDIA in its FQ227 (Jul) 10-Q conveyed:
"The availability of land, power, shell, and capital is crucial to support the buildout of a
full data center inclusive of NVIDIA AI infrastructure by our customers and partners, and
any shortage of these or other necessary resources could impact our future revenue and
financial performance. Expanding land, power, shell, and energy needs to meet demand
is a complex, multi-year process that involves significant regulatory, technical, and
construction challenges. In addition, access to capital can be particularly constrained for
less-capitalized companies, which may face difficulties securing financing for large-scale
infrastructure projects."
UBS Evidence Lab currently identifies approximately 201 GW of global data center
capacity under construction or planned globally, including 126GW in the US. This
provides meaningful support for the nearer-term build-out, but our model requires a
further step-up in projects moving from planning into permitting and construction later
in the decade. In particular, 2029-30 becomes as much about power availability as
semiconductor and component supply.
